text: Chapter one named feature store as the first platform component. This lesson explains the actual problem it solves, before we get into online and offline splits and architecture patterns. If you've ever seen a model behave worse in production than its test metrics suggested, there's a good chance the cause is exactly what we're covering here.

Without a feature store, a feature like a driver's average rating over the last seven days usually gets computed twice, by two different pieces of code written at two different times. Training-time code is a batch query over historical data. Serving-time code is a fast function running on live data for every prediction request. Both are supposed to compute the same value, but in practice they drift — someone fixes a bug in one and forgets the other, or the two handle an edge case differently. That gap is called training-serving skew, covered fully in lesson eight.

A feature store lets you define a feature once, as code, and get two things automatically from that single definition: a way to compute its historical values for training sets, and a way to serve its latest value fast enough for a live prediction. The key point is that one definition drives both paths — a shared table of pre-computed values isn't enough on its own if separate logic still populates it for training versus serving.

Feast is the most widely adopted open-source feature store. A feature starts as a FeatureView definition in Python — here it's keyed on driver id, points at a parquet file as its source, and exposes fields like conversion rate and acceptance rate. This single definition tells Feast where the data lives, what entity it's keyed on, and what it exposes, and it's what drives both the training path and the serving path, which lesson six covers in detail.

A feature store is also a governance tool, not just a performance one — once a feature is defined in one place, a new model reuses it instead of reinventing it, and a bug fix benefits every model using it at once. Up next, lesson six: exactly how that one definition splits into an online path and an offline path.
